title: Sign of a permutation on two ordered complementary blocks
statement:
Let $q\ge0$ and $0\le s\le q$ be integers and write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$, with $[0]=\varnothing$. For each $m$, let $S_m$ be the permutations of $[m]$ and let $\operatorname{sgn}:S_m\to\{\pm1\}\subset\mathbf Z$ be the homomorphism taking each transposition to $-1$, as defined in [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Let $T,I\subseteq[q]$ have size $s$ and list them increasingly as $T=(t_1,\ldots,t_s)$ and $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_s)$. List their complements increasingly as $T^c=(u_1,\ldots,u_{q-s})$ and $I^c=(v_1,\ldots,v_{q-s})$. If $\sigma\in S_q$ satisfies $\sigma(T)=I$, define $\alpha\in S_s$ and $\beta\in S_{q-s}$ by $\sigma(t_a)=i_{\alpha(a)}$ and $\sigma(u_b)=v_{\beta(b)}$. Then
$$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^{\sum_{i\in I}i+\sum_{t\in T}t}\operatorname{sgn}(\alpha)\operatorname{sgn}(\beta)\quad\text{in }\mathbf Z.$$
The assertion includes $s=0$, $s=q$ and $q=0$, with the sign of the unique empty permutation equal to $1$.

proof.text: For each $s$-element subset $A\subseteq[q]$, with increasing lists $A=(a_1,\ldots,a_s)$ and $A^c=(c_1,\ldots,c_{q-s})$, define the permutation $\rho_A$ by $\rho_A(j)=a_j$ for $1\le j\le s$ and $\rho_A(s+b)=c_b$ for $1\le b\le q-s$. The lists are disjoint and exhaust $[q]$, so this is a bijection. Since $\sigma$ is bijective and maps $T$ onto $I$, it maps $T^c$ onto $I^c$. Thus the displayed rules in the statement define bijections $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Put $\delta=\rho_I^{-1}\circ\sigma\circ\rho_T$. Evaluating on the two blocks gives $\delta(j)=\alpha(j)$ and $\delta(s+b)=s+\beta(b)$; equivalently $\sigma=\rho_I\circ\delta\circ\rho_T^{-1}$.

source.place: Tag 07Z7, lemma-ideals-generated-by-minors, proof lines 1350-1352: omitted determinant expansion hint; the ordered-shuffle calculation below is supplied by Q54, not asserted by Stacks.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-permutation-sign-inversion-product] to $\rho_A$, first for $A=T$ and then for $A=I$. That node is stated for permutations of $\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$; transport along the order-preserving bijection $x\mapsto x-1$ from $[m]$ sends transpositions to transpositions, so it preserves $\operatorname{sgn}$ and all order comparisons, and the same product formula holds for permutations of $[m]$. Both image blocks in its defining list are increasing, so their internal pair factors are $1$. For the cross pairs with first entry $j\le s$, the factor is $-1$ exactly when $c_b<a_j$. Of the $a_j-1$ integers below $a_j$, exactly $j-1$ belong to $A$; hence exactly $a_j-j$ belong to $A^c$. Regrouping these factors gives $$\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_A)=(-1)^{e_A},\qquad e_A=\sum_{j=1}^s(a_j-j)=\sum_{a\in A}a-\frac{s(s+1)}2.$$ Each $a_j\ge j$, so these exponents are nonnegative. This is a count of the factors in the cited product, with no shuffle-sign identity assumed.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-permutation-sign-inversion-product] (with the same relabelling as in step 2) to $\delta$, $\alpha$ and $\beta$. In the product for $\delta$, a pair meeting both position blocks has image in the same block order: $\alpha(j)\le s<s+\beta(b)$. All such factors equal $1$. For pairs within the first block, the factors are exactly those for $\alpha$. Within the second block, subtracting $s$ from the two arguments and their images gives exactly the factors for $\beta$. Partitioning the finite product into these three disjoint sets of pairs therefore yields $$\operatorname{sgn}(\delta)=\operatorname{sgn}(\alpha)\operatorname{sgn}(\beta).$$ This also applies when either block is empty.

source.place: Tag 07Z7, lemma-ideals-generated-by-minors, proof lines 1350-1352: omitted determinant expansion hint; the ordered-shuffle calculation below is supplied by Q54, not asserted by Stacks.

proof.text: The sign is a homomorphism by [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], so the identity from step 1 and steps 2-3 give $$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)=(-1)^{e_I+e_T}\operatorname{sgn}(\alpha)\operatorname{sgn}(\beta).$$ Here $\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_T^{-1})=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_T)$, because a sign is $1$ or $-1$, its own inverse. The integer $e_I+e_T$ equals $\sum_{i\in I}i+\sum_{t\in T}t-s(s+1)$. The subtracted integer is even, since one of $s,s+1$ is even, so the power of $-1$ is the one asserted in the statement. If $s=0$, both shuffles are the identity, $\alpha$ is empty and $\beta=\sigma$. If $s=q$, both shuffles are again the identity, $\beta$ is empty and $\alpha=\sigma$; the exponent is $q(q+1)$, which is even. If $q=0$, every permutation is the identity on the empty set and a homomorphism sends it to $1$. Thus every boundary case has the stated convention.
